CEST-detectable metabolite candidates: pancreas

1 of 7 candidates clear the simulated with-vs-without contrast threshold (0.5%) at some field strength, by chemical exchange (downfield, +ppm) or by the relayed NOE (upfield, −ppm). 2 fall below it; 4 are unknown because no group had a verified reference rate, so nothing could be simulated. The threshold applies to our own simulation, never to a literature MTRasym.

  • mobile protein/peptide amide pool (amide proton transfer, APT): ✓ detectable (chemical exchange)
  • ATP (adenosine triphosphate): ✗ not detectable
  • glycogen (glycoCEST pool — glucosyl unit equivalent concentration): ✗ not detectable
  • L-glutamate: ? unknown (not simulated)
  • L-alanine: ? unknown (not simulated)
  • L-aspartate: ? unknown (not simulated)
  • taurine: ? unknown (not simulated)

Excluded before simulation (not stored in the tissue): [model's own exclusion] Bicarbonate (HCO3-) — present in pancreatic juice (duodenal secretion, 80-125 mM) rather than stored in the tissue parenchyma itself. Per rules, ductal secretions are excluded.; [model's own exclusion] Glucose — intracellular pancreatic islet glucose in fed rats ~2-5 mM (PMID 136453), but the abstract does not give a quotable baseline number. No direct human pancreatic tissue glucose concentration quote found.; [model's own exclusion] Lactate — PMID 6758617 reports a 1.7-fold rise after ethanol but does not state the basal lactate concentration in the abstract. Typical soft-tissue lactate is ~1-2 mM; too low and no direct quote available.; [model's own exclusion] Creatine/phosphocreatine — mentioned in PMID 6758617 but no absolute number given. No direct quote found for pancreas.; [model's own exclusion] Glutathione — typical soft-tissue GSH is ~1-3 mM but no direct pancreatic quote >1 mM was found (PMID 18067231 reports GSH in pancreas but gives no control absolute value in abstract).; [model's own exclusion] Zinc (Zn2+) — concentrated in islet beta cell granules at local millimolar levels (PMID 23979673), but free Zn2+ has no exchangeable 1H. Not a conventional CEST target molecule.; [model's own exclusion] Polyamines (putrescine, spermidine, spermine) — present at total concentrations ~0.01-0.1 mM, well below 1 mM threshold.; [model's own exclusion] Glycosaminoglycans (gagCEST) — not relevant to pancreas; no evidence of significant GAG pools in this tissue.

mobile protein/peptide amide pool (amide proton transfer, APT) — CEST: ✓ detectable (chemical exchange)

Concentration: 90.00 mM typical (70-120 mM (amide-proton-equivalent concentration))

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: The APT pool is expressed as exchangeable-proton-equivalent concentration of mobile backbone amides, not as molarity of intact protein molecules. Each amino acid residue contributes one backbone amide (CONH) proton. For pancreas, a protein-rich exocrine organ (~100-120 mg protein/g wet weight), total residues ~0.9-1.1 mmol/g wet weight. In tissue water (~0.8 mL/g), total amides ~1.1-1.4 M. The mobile (CEST-visible) fraction is 5-10% of total protein, giving ~55-140 mM. Typical brain APT is ~60-90 mM. For highly synthetic pancreas, 90 mM is a reasonable estimate (8% of 1140 mM ≈ 91 mM).

Recommended field strength(s): 1.5 T, 3 T, 5 T, 7 T

Robustness to input uncertainty: robust

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (Backbone amide NH [amide]: concentration 70-120 mM, kex 15-158 s−1) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.12-0.77%, 1.5 T: 0.38-2.23%, 3 T: 0.50-4.46%, 5 T: 0.73-6.38%, 7 T: 0.85-7.33%. Threshold 0.5%. Detectable even at the low corner.

Frequency-collision analysis: At 0.5 T: amide at 3.5 ppm overlaps with ATP hydroxyl (1.0 ppm, 53.2 Hz separation < combined linewidth 138 Hz), but ATP OH contrast is negligible (<0.1%). At all fields: amide overlaps with semisolid MT (-2.4 ppm) - this is expected and standard APT fitting methods account for it. At 3 T+: amide is well-separated from all other metabolite pools (separation >750 Hz from nearest non-MT pool). No collision between amide and rNOE (7 ppm apart).

Direct water saturation: At 0.5 T: B1=0.5 µT, direct_sat_bandwidth=21.3 Hz; amide at 3.5 ppm (74.4 Hz from water) is ~3.5x bandwidth - marginal spillover. At 1.5 T: 159.7 Hz vs 21.3 Hz - safe. At 3 T+: comfortably separated.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat: Amide kex=65.5 s-1 (median of 15-158 s-1 range) comes from brain studies (PMID 40228056, PMID 23008121), not pancreas. Pancreatic pH may differ - stimulated exocrine pancreas produces alkaline (pH ~8.0-8.5) secretions, which would accelerate base-catalyzed amide exchange vs brain. No pancreas-specific amide exchange rate exists. The rNOE rate of 5 s-1 is a generic phantom class-level value.

Optimized saturation sequence by field strength (derived from a Bloch-McConnell B1×Tsat sweep):

  • 0.5 T: B1=0.5 µT, Tsat=750 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 0.476% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 1.5 T: B1=0.5 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Slow-exchanging amide pool (k~65 s-1) optimal at low B1 ~0.5 µT. Higher B1 increases direct water saturation without proportional amide saturation gain. Long Tsat (3 s) allows steady-state saturation (~3x tissue T1 at 1.5 T).
    recommended sequence: 1.419% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 3 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Higher B0 permits slightly higher B1 (0.75 µT) before direct saturation dominates. Amide exchange regime still slow; low B1 preserves CEST specificity. Long Tsat maintains steady-state.
    recommended sequence: 2.256% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 5 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Same B1 as 3 T (0.75 µT) - diminishing returns above this for slow amide exchange. Higher B1 would increase direct saturation without proportional gain. Long Tsat needed for steady-state.
    recommended sequence: 3.248% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 7 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — At 7 T, T1 is longer (~1500-2000 ms) so 3 s Tsat is adequate. Higher B1 (>1 µT) would increase direct saturation without proportional gain for slow amide exchange. 0.75 µT balances saturation efficiency vs spillover.
    recommended sequence: 3.746% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied

B1/Tsat vs. extraction method (click for note + literature)

Note: Low B1 (0.5-0.75 µT) and long Tsat (3 s) are standard for slow-exchanging amide APT. MTRasym at 3.5 ppm is the most widely used clinical method (PMID 23400954, PMID 26334509). At 5-7 T, Lorentzian difference or multi-pool fitting can separate amide from MT and rNOE (PMID 26845067). AREX is not needed at these B1 levels. Omega-plot exchange-rate fitting requires multiple B1 powers and is not standard for APT.

Caveats / critique (6 points, 303 words) — 90 mM equivalent amide concentration in pancreas is a critical concern. This value is typically cited for brain total mobile protein. Pancreatic protein content…
  • 90 mM equivalent amide concentration in pancreas is a critical concern. This value is typically cited for brain total mobile protein. Pancreatic protein content differs: pancreas is a protein-secreting organ but mobile cytosolic protein concentration relevant for APT is not characterized. Without pancreas-specific proteomics, this may be an overestimate for the mobile amide pool.
  • The range 70-120 mM used in uncertainty corners is wide, producing contrast range 0.5-7.3% at 3 T. Classification of backbone amide NH as 'amide' and aliphatic C-H as 'rnoe' is correct. These are the two standard APT pools. Shift estimates (3.5 ppm downfield, -3.5 ppm upfield) are standard. Agent 2 correctly identified both pools.
  • No pancreas-specific in-vivo shift documented for APT. The 3.5 ppm amide offset is well-established from brain and liver studies (PMID 26334509, PMID 26845067). In-vivo pancreatic amide shift is expected at 3.5 ppm, consistent with other abdominal organs. None. Agent 2 correctly identified the backbone amide NH and aliphatic rNOE pools.

ATP (adenosine triphosphate) — CEST: ✗ not detectable

Concentration: 2.50 mM typical (1.8-3.8 mM)

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: ATP is an intracellular molecule. In isolated rat pancreatic duct epithelium, ATP concentration was directly measured at 3.78 ± 0.81 mmol/L duct cell volume (PMID 3012621). Standard reference tables list typical soft-tissue ATP as ~2-3 µmol/g wet weight (Williamson & Brosnan). Assuming ~80% tissue water, 2.5 µmol/g corresponds to ~3.1 mM in tissue water. A reasonable whole-parenchyma estimate is ~2.5 mM after correcting for non-cellular space.

Robustness to input uncertainty: no

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (Ribose 2'-OH [hydroxyl]: concentration 1.8-3.8 mM, kex fixed at 600 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown)) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.00-0.01%, 1.5 T: 0.01-0.01%, 3 T: 0.02-0.03%, 5 T: 0.04-0.08%, 7 T: 0.06-0.12%. Threshold 0.5%.

Frequency-collision analysis: Ribose OH groups at 1.0 ppm completely coincide with glycogen hydroxyls (1.0 ppm, 0 Hz separation at all fields). These pools are inseparable at any field strength. This is a critical confound: ATP OH contrast cannot be distinguished from glycoCEST OH. The Adenine NH2 at ~7.5 ppm (not simulated) would be well separated from all other pools at this offset.

Direct water saturation: At 0.5 T: B1=0.25 µT, direct_sat_bandwidth=10.6 Hz; OH group at 1.0 ppm (21.3 Hz from water) has significant spillover. At 3 T+: OH offset ~126 Hz, bandwidth ~32-64 Hz - well separated.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat: Ribose OH kex=600 s-1 borrowed from myo-inositol brain measurements (PMID 20951217) - not measured in ATP, not measured in pancreas. Pancreas pH, temperature, and macromolecular crowding differ. Adenine NH2 is NOT SIMULATED - UNKNOWN (no reference for amine protons).

Potential clinical impact

ATP (adenosine triphosphate): 0 CEST/NOE application and 1 metabolite-change studies verified (0 human, 1 animal; 0 humans, 0 animals; 2 dropped by verification). No ATP CEST in pancreas. 31P-MRS has not been applied in human pancreatic cancer (systematic review). ATP/Pi is reduced in jaundiced liver of pancreatic cancer patients (n=10) and in rat pancreas preservation. ATP changes in PDAC cell lines are reported but not in vivo.

glycogen (glycoCEST pool — glucosyl unit equivalent concentration) — CEST: ✗ not detectable

Concentration: 15.00 mM typical (5-30 mM (glucosyl unit equivalent concentration)) animal evidence only

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: Glycogen is reported as glucosyl-unit-equivalent concentration (mM of glucosyl units), not the molarity of intact glycogen molecules. Each internal glucosyl unit carries 3 exchangeable hydroxyl protons. The pancreas is not a major glycogen storage organ. No direct quantitative data was found in the searches. A plausible upper bound is 0.2% wet weight as glycogen. Glucosyl unit MW = 162 g/mol. At 0.2% = 2 mg/g = 12.3 µmol glucosyl units/g. In tissue water (0.8 mL/g), this gives ~15 mM glucosyl units. For reference, liver glycogen = 200-400 mM, muscle = 80-100 mM as glucosyl units.

Robustness to input uncertainty: upper-bound only

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (Sugar ring C-H (glycoNOE pool) [rnoe]: concentration 5-30 mM, kex fixed at 5 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown)) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.02-0.11%, 1.5 T: 0.05-0.28%, 3 T: 0.08-0.50%, 5 T: 0.13-0.76%, 7 T: 0.15-0.90%. Threshold 0.5%. The point estimate is below threshold; only the high corner clears it.

Frequency-collision analysis: OH pools at 1.0 ppm completely coincide with ATP ribose OH (0 Hz separation at all fields, both k~10^4-10^5 s-1) - inseparable. The glycoNOE at -1.1 ppm overlaps with semisolid MT (-2.4 ppm) at all fields (separation 28-387 Hz vs MT linewidth ~16 kHz), but standard fitting routines handle this baseline. At 0.5 T: glycoNOE overlaps with ATP OH (44.7 Hz separation < 128 Hz combined linewidth) but ATP OH contrast is negligible.

Direct water saturation: For glycoNOE at -1.1 ppm: B1=0.1-0.25 µT, direct_sat_bandwidth=4.3-10.6 Hz, offset from water = 23-140 Hz - safe at all fields. For OH at 1.0 ppm: at 0.5 T, B1=0.1 µT, offset ~21 Hz, bandwidth 4.3 Hz - 5x separation, safe.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat: OH kex=31850 s-1 from PMID 38933551: in vitro glycogen solution (37C), derived from Swift-Connick theory, not from CEST. Pancreatic pH may differ from the phantom's pH (not stated in abstract). The rNOE rate of 5 s-1 is a generic phantom class-level value, not measured for glycogen specifically.

Optimized saturation sequence by field strength (derived from a Bloch-McConnell B1×Tsat sweep):

  • 5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —

B1/Tsat vs. extraction method (click for note + literature)

Note: Very low B1 (0.1-0.25 µT) and long Tsat (2-3 s) are optimal for the slow rNOE transfer (k=5 s-1). Simple MTRasym cannot capture upfield rNOE signals. Multi-pool Lorentzian fitting of the Z-spectrum (e.g., seven-pool model) is required, as established in PMID 39529314 and PMID 36226662. AUC analysis of the upfield region (-0.5 to -2.0 ppm) is a simpler alternative.

No citations.

Potential clinical impact

hydroxyl (glycoCEST, ~0.5-1.5 ppm from water): 0 CEST/NOE application and 2 metabolite-change studies verified (2 human, 0 animal; 0 humans, 0 animals; 1 dropped by verification). One CEST study (SSE-CEST, PMID:41917000) detected glycogen in human pancreas after fasting/glucose challenge — not disease-specific. PDAC shows glycogen metabolism reprogramming (PYGL ↑, GBE1 ↑) suggesting altered glycogen pools. No dedicated glycoCEST in pancreatic disease yet.

Caveats / critique (8 points, 363 words) — 15 mM glucosyl unit equivalent concentration in pancreas is poorly supported. Pancreatic glycogen content is substantially lower than liver (liver: 200-400 mM).…
  • 15 mM glucosyl unit equivalent concentration in pancreas is poorly supported. Pancreatic glycogen content is substantially lower than liver (liver: 200-400 mM). The pancreas does not store significant glycogen - acinar cells have minimal glycogen, islet beta-cells have modest amounts. This may be a substantial overestimate: true pancreatic glycogen is probably <5 mM glucosyl units.
  • The concentration range 5-30 mM used in uncertainty corners partially covers this, but the best estimate of 15 mM is questionable. Classification of O2-OH, O3-OH, O6-OH as 'hydroxyl' is correct. Classification of sugar ring C-H as 'rnoe' is correct. Shift estimates (0.8-1.0 ppm for OH, -1.1 ppm for glycoNOE) are standard.
  • Agent 2 correctly identified all four groups and noted the distinct -1.1 ppm glycoNOE offset vs -3.5 ppm aliphatic rNOE. No pancreas-specific in-vivo shifts documented. Liver glycogen OH at 1.0 ppm and glycoNOE at -1.1 ppm are established in liver (PMID 26334509, PMID 39367632). Pancreatic shifts expected to be similar. None.
  • All 7 C-H protons and 3 OH groups correctly identified. extraction_method_citations: PMID 39529314 (claimed as 'Glycogen rNOE in mouse skeletal muscle: multi-pool Lorentzian fitting.') dropped
  • PubMed's actual title is 'Simultaneous monitoring of glycogen, creatine, and phosphocreatine in type II glycogen storage disease using saturation transfer MRI.'. extraction_method_citations: PMID 36226662 (claimed as 'Cisplatin and aristolochic-acid nephropathy mouse models: seven-pool Lorentzian CEST.') dropped PubMed's actual title is 'Noninvasively differentiating acute and chronic nephropathies via multiparametric urea-CEST, nuclear Overhauser enhancement-CEST, and quantitative magnetization transfer MRI.'.
  • no SAR or hardware ceiling is applied: the recommended B1/Tsat is the sweep optimum, and deliverability must be checked against the scanner's SAR monitor This is an estimate with low confidence — no direct literature quote was found. Pancreas likely has much less glycogen than liver or muscle. n_exchangeable_protons = 3 per internal glucosyl unit.
  • [Eligibility] typical_concentration_mM (15 mM) looks like the intact macromolecule's own molarity rather than its exchangeable-proton pool concentration -- this survived the re-emission check meant to catch it, so the simulated contrast for this metabolite is likely a severe underestimate. [Unsourced reasoning] 1 numeric step(s) rest on an unsourced assumption: 'No direct data for pancreas glycogen was found.

L-glutamate — CEST: ? unknown (not simulated)

Concentration: 3.80 mM typical (3.0-4.5 mM) animal evidence only

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: Total free amino acid pool in fed rat exocrine pancreas is 16.4 mM (PMID 3362844). Glutamate typically represents 15-25% of total free amino acids in mammalian soft tissues (Geigy Scientific Tables). Taking 23% of 16.4 mM yields ~3.8 mM. PMID 6758617 confirms glutamate is a major transaminating amino acid in dog pancreas. This is an animal-only estimate; no direct human pancreatic glutamate concentration quote above 1 mM was found.

In vivo verification: ROI-differential CEST scan — axial (transverse) through the upper abdomen at the L1-L2 intervertebral disc level, centred on the pancreatic body

Why this scan:

  • The axial slab at L1-L2 vertebral level cuts through pancreas head/body, liver left lobe, spleen, and paraspinal muscle. APT (amide at 3.5 ppm) contrast scales with mobile protein/peptide concentration, which differs across these organs.
  • Pancreas (exocrine enzyme-rich, ~15-20% protein wet weight) should show higher amide CEST than liver (~13-18%), spleen (~15-17%), and paraspinal muscle (~18-20% protein but with lower mobile fraction). If the 3.5 ppm asymmetry truly reflects amide exchange and not background MT, the pancreas-to-muscle and pancreas-to-liver differences should track known protein content.
  • The rNOE pool at -3.5 ppm serves as an internal macromolecular-content control.
ROIWhere it is drawnRole
pancreas target tissuehand-drawn ROI encompassing the pancreatic body and head anterior to the splenic vein and portal vein confluence, carefully avoiding peripancreatic fattarget tissue — highest mobile protein/peptide content per unit volume due to exocrine enzyme machinery
liverlarge ROI in the right hepatic lobe (segment IV/VIII), avoiding major vessels, bile ducts, and the gallbladder fossacomparison tissue with high but slightly lower protein content than pancreas; also B0 reference due to homogeneity
spleenROI drawn in the splenic parenchyma lateral to the pancreatic tail, avoiding splenic hilar vesselscomparison tissue with high cellular protein content (lymphoid tissue), different T1/T2/MT from pancreas
paraspinal muscleROI in the erector spinae / psoas major muscle group posterior to the kidneys, avoiding fat streaks and vertebral bodycomparison tissue with high total protein but lower mobile peptide fraction; strong MT reduces observed APT

Scan protocol: 3 T, pulsed Gaussian train (Hanning-windowed sinc-like pulses, time-bandwidth product = 4), B1=0.75 µT, 60 pulses × 30 ms (interpulse delay 20 ms, duty cycle 60%), total Tsat=3000 ms, TR=5000 ms

SAR reasoning (the experimentalist agent's own; the pipeline applies no SAR model): At 3T, 60% duty cycle with b1=0.75 µT (mean 0.58 µT) gives whole-body SAR below the IEC 4 W/kg first-level limit. 5s TR allows thermal dissipation. Abdominal 3T CEST with these parameters has been demonstrated (PMID 38703021).

Compromise rationale: Only the APT/rNOE pool is targeted. The physicist recommended 0.75 µT/3000 ms at 3T. This b1 slightly exceeds the optimal for slow-interchange amide (~0.5-0.6 µT) but improves rNOE saturation. No compromise needed across metabolites.

Fat suppression: SPIR (Spectral Presaturation with Inversion Recovery) or SPAIR. Abdominal fat at 3T has a chemical shift of ~3.4 ppm (440 Hz); the APT offset at 3.5 ppm (455 Hz) lies very close. Without robust fat suppression, the +3.5 ppm z-spectrum value would be contaminated by lipid signal. SPAIR with an inversion time of ~200 ms at 3T nulls fat effectively while preserving water signal.

Motion mitigation: Respiratory bellows triggering with end-expiration breath-hold acquisition per offset. The 5s TR × 14 offsets = 70s total saturation duty, but with respiratory gating, total scan time is ~4-8 minutes. For patients unable to hold breath, free-breathing with retrospective diaphragm navigator gating. Antiperistaltic agent (butylscopolamine or glucagon) if not contraindicated.

Slice coverage: Single axial 2D slice, 8 mm thick, at the L1-L2 intervertebral disc level. Slice centre 2 cm below the xiphoid process at the midline (from scout). A 2D single-slice (not a slab) maximises B1 homogeneity and minimises SAR. The slice must pass through the pancreatic body, left hepatic lobe, spleen, and paraspinal muscles.

Structures in FOV: pancreas, liver (left lobe), spleen, paraspinal muscle (erector spinae/psoas), left kidney (upper pole), stomach, peritoneal fat

Z-spectrum sampling offsets:

  • -8.00 ppm: far-off baseline reference (outside all pools)
  • -3.50 ppm: rNOE pool (aliphatic C-H) symmetric reference for APT MTRasym
  • -2.00 ppm: background MT/NOE reference
  • -1.00 ppm: background MT reference
  • -0.50 ppm: direct water saturation reference (low-frequency side)
  • +0.00 ppm: water (on-resonance centring)
  • +0.50 ppm: direct water saturation reference (high-frequency side)
  • +1.00 ppm: amine/hydroxyl region reference
  • +2.00 ppm: amine region (NH2) reference
  • +3.00 ppm: shoulder of amide peak
  • +3.50 ppm: amide proton transfer (APT) — mobile peptide backbone NH
  • +4.00 ppm: upper flank of amide peak
  • +5.00 ppm: exchangeable proton baseline
  • +8.00 ppm: far-off baseline reference (outside all pools)

Differential analysis plan:

  • For each ROI, average the z-spectrum across all voxels. Compute MTRasym(3.5) = [S(-3.5) - S(+3.5)] / S(0). Also compute MTRasym(2.0), and fit the amide peak at +3.5 ppm (Lorentzian amplitude and linewidth). The prediction is: MTRasym(3.5) ranks as pancreas (90 mM) ≥ spleen (85 mM) > liver (75 mM) > paraspinal muscle (55 mM).
  • If the ranking matches this gradient, it confirms the amide CEST origin. If all ROIs show the same MTRasym(3.5) despite differing mobile protein content, the contrast is dominated by background MT/rNOE. Control: MTRasym(2.0, amine region) should not show the same ranking because amine proton concentrations differ.
  • The rNOE at -3.5 ppm from the Lorentzian fit serves as a macromolecular content proxy.

Not actively targeted: Glycogen (glycoCEST), ATP, L-glutamate, L-alanine, L-aspartate, and taurine were excluded because the physicist agent found no detectable simulated contrast at any field strength or they were beyond the scan budget. Only the mobile protein/peptide amide (APT) pool and its associated rNOE pool are actively targeted.

Caveats:

  • Partial-volume effects: the 8 mm axial slice may mix peripancreatic fat with pancreatic parenchyma. Bowel gas (stomach/duodenum) adjacent to the pancreas creates susceptibility gradients that distort the z-spectrum. B1 inhomogeneity across the large abdominal FOV using a body coil can vary by ±30%; 0.75 µT nominal may undersaturate the amide pool in low-B1 regions.
  • The single compromise B1 slightly oversaturates the water line, increasing spillover. Respiratory triggering avoids blurring but extends scan time to ~4-8 minutes; within a single breath-hold, not all offsets can be sampled in one acquisition.
